items.title: Jefferson Einstein Philadelphia and Montgomery: MyEinsteinHealth ends Sept. 26, 2026
items.dek: Official Jefferson page: MyEinsteinHealth migrates to MyJeffersonHealth, the Epic MyChart portal, for Jefferson Einstein Philadelphia and Jefferson Einstein Montgomery.
items.body:
Beginning Sept. 26, 2026, Jefferson Health says Einstein Healthcare Network electronic health records will migrate from MyEinsteinHealth to MyJeffersonHealth, Jefferson Health’s patient portal powered by Epic’s MyChart. The same page says Einstein Healthcare Network is now part of Jefferson Health and includes Jefferson Einstein Philadelphia Hospital and Jefferson Einstein Montgomery Hospital.

The page says clinicians at those two hospitals are moving to the Epic electronic health record system. After Sept. 26, 2026, patients will no longer access MyEinsteinHealth. Records will be available in MyJeffersonHealth after the next visit to a clinician at either Einstein hospital. Jefferson says it will move up to three years of MyEinsteinHealth records.
items.impactSentence: After Sept. 26, 2026, patients will no longer access MyEinsteinHealth; records are in MyJeffersonHealth (Epic MyChart) after the next visit to either Einstein hospital, with up to three years of records moved.
items.contextSentence: Jefferson and Einstein completed their merger in October 2021, making this portal and EHR cutover a later operational milestone in the systems’ integration.

items.title: 84 Del. Laws ch. 408, effective Sept. 19, 2024: PBM 340B nondiscrimination
items.dek: HS 1 for HB 383 bars pharmacy benefits managers and purchasers from discriminating against 340B covered entities. A below-NADAC 340B rate is one listed practice. Violations are unfair insurance practices. Later contracts with those terms are void.
items.body:
84 Del. Laws ch. 408, House Substitute 1 for House Bill 383, took effect Sept. 19, 2024. The Delaware General Assembly bill was signed that day. It amends Titles 18 and 24 of the Delaware Code on 340B drugs and covered entities.

Section 2 adds 18 Del. C. § 3374A. A pharmacy benefits manager or purchaser may not discriminate against a covered entity or its contracted pharmacy because it participates in the federal 340B program under 42 U.S.C. § 256b. Covered entity means as defined in 42 U.S.C. § 256b(a)(4).

One listed practice is a reimbursement rate for a 340B drug that is less than the national average drug acquisition cost rate determined by CMS, measured when the drug is administered or dispensed, or less than wholesale acquisition cost if that NADAC rate is unavailable.

A violation of § 3374A(b) is an unfair practice in the insurance business. A contract entered into, amended, extended, or renewed after Sept. 19, 2024 that includes a provision that violates that subsection is void and unenforceable.
items.impactSentence: 84 Del. Laws ch. 408 (HS 1 for HB 383) took effect Sept. 19, 2024 and bars a PBM or purchaser from paying a 340B covered entity less than the CMS NADAC rate, or WAC if NADAC is unavailable.

HS 1 for HB 383 engrossment, 18 Del. C. 3374A

items.contextSentence: HS 1 for HB 383 became 84 Del. Laws ch. 408 when it was signed and took effect Sept. 19, 2024.

items.title: ChristianaCare Epic go-live, official July 2026 update
items.dek: ChristianaCare’s Oct. 3, 2026 Epic cutover follows a role-based training and readiness program described in the system’s July update.
items.body: ChristianaCare’s July 2026 newsroom update scheduled an Oct. 3, 2026 Epic go-live and said the system was in the final stage, with less than three months remaining. COO Ric Cuming said training mixes on-demand modules with live, role-based instruction, and that readiness checks are meant to make sure caregivers finish required training before they use the new system. The same update said that once ChristianaCare is live, all Delaware health systems — and many in Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Maryland — will be on Epic, with Care Everywhere for outside visits. Patients are told to keep appointments unless ChristianaCare contacts them. Becker’s Hospital Review, Naomi Diaz, Wednesday, July 22, 2026, also reported the Oct. 3 date and said the EHR switch has been underway since a 2024 decision. It names Robert Hartmann, vice president of EHR transformation, who spent nine years at Epic.
items.impactSentence: ChristianaCare’s Oct. 3 Epic cutover is tied to role-based training and readiness checks for caregivers.
items.contextSentence: ChristianaCare’s Epic program has been underway since a 2024 decision; the July 2026 newsroom update fixed the Oct. 3 go-live date.

items.title: Jefferson FY2026 operating loss and Fitch liquidity
items.dek: The Inquirer reported a $181.5 million FY2026 operating loss, including $112 million for layoffs and other moves; Fitch cited $5.5 billion of unrestricted liquidity and 119 days cash on hand through March 31.
items.body:
The Inquirer, Aug. 14, 2026, reported that Thomas Jefferson University and Jefferson Health posted a $181.5 million operating loss for the year ended June 30, 2026, after a $208 million loss the prior year, in results reported to bondholders.

The same clip said those FY2026 results included $112 million in costs for layoffs and other moves. Jefferson completed the Lehigh Valley Health Network close on Aug. 1, 2024; the Inquirer said FY2025 revenue included 11 months of LVHN and rose to $17.7 billion in FY2026 from $15.8 billion.

Jefferson Health Plans lost $130.3 million on 415,172 members. Results climbed from a $103.8 million first-quarter operating loss to a $71.1 million fourth-quarter operating profit. CFO Michael Harrington said commercial-insurer actions in Pennsylvania threaten those gains. Jefferson sued Independence Blue Cross over contract reinterpretations and sued Aetna in April over Medicare Advantage stay payments. Independence said it acts for its customers. Aetna said its policies comply with federal law.

Separately, Fitch on June 18, 2026 assigned F1+ to TJU taxable CP notes, affirmed the A IDR with a Negative Outlook, and cited $5.5 billion unrestricted liquidity and about 119 days cash on hand for fiscal 2026 year-to-date through March 31, 2026, including the health plan and excluding line-of-credit draws and about $1.1 billion donor-restricted funds. Fitch cited about $15.5 billion operating revenue for the year ended June 30, 2025, and about $112 million Jefferson Health Plan losses through the first nine months of both FY2025 and FY2026.
items.impactSentence: The $181.5 million year-end operating loss sits next to $5.5 billion / 119 DCOH through March 31; Harrington says the climb holds only if commercial contracts do.
items.contextSentence: Jefferson completed the Lehigh Valley Health Network close on Aug. 1, 2024; the Inquirer said FY2026 is the first full year of combined results.

items.title: Penn in-house scribe headcount and 2024 JAMA pilot table
items.dek: The Inquirer reported roughly 1,200 ambulatory users of Penn’s in-house scribe. A separate 46-clinician 2024 quality-improvement study evaluated DAX Copilot.
items.body:
The Philadelphia Inquirer, Nov. 10, 2025, said Dina Capalongo, a Penn Medicine internist, uses an AI scribe Penn designed in-house: she hits a green button on a phone app, ambient listening drafts a sectioned note she still has to approve, usually before she leaves the room. The same clip said some 1,200 Penn Medicine providers were using the in-house scribe in ambulatory and outpatient offices. Mitchell Schnall said the system built the tool.

A separate JAMA Network Open study (Duggan et al., published Feb. 19, 2025; outpatient QI April–June 2024 at one Philadelphia academic system) evaluated DAX Copilot (Nuance) among 46 clinicians in 17 specialties. The abstract associated that tool with 20.4% less time in notes per appointment (10.3 to 8.2 minutes; P<.001), 9.3% greater same-day appointment closure (66.2% to 72.4%), and 30.0% less after-hours work time (50.6 to 35.4 minutes per workday). Penn Medicine’s Feb. 21, 2025 news release called the early results promising and said volunteer clinicians used the tool with patient permission.
items.impactSentence: Penn’s in-house scribe reached roughly 1,200 ambulatory users; a separate 46-clinician DAX Copilot study reported 20.4% less note time per appointment.
items.contextSentence: The 1,200-user in-house scribe count is from the Nov. 10, 2025 Inquirer clip; the DAX Copilot percentages are a separate 46-clinician JAMA Network Open study.

items.body:
HealthTech Magazine, August 2026, said Benjamin Slovis has a Microsoft Dragon Copilot rollout to 400 end users and quoted him that the tool is “not yet a silver bullet.” HealthTech identified him as chief medical information officer at Philadelphia-based Temple Health. Temple’s June 8, 2026 newsroom note, which names him Chief Medical Information Officer for Temple University Hospital, said he described Dragon Ambient eXperience (DAX) Copilot to the Bucks County Herald: it records the visit and drafts a note the doctor reviews.

A Temple-sponsored Philadelphia Business Journal article from April 1, 2026 names Slovis as CMIO at Temple University Hospital and reports that the pilot reduced after-hours documentation time by more than 10 percent. The same article said the rollout had expanded to nearly 400 physicians.
items.impactSentence: Temple expanded Dragon Copilot to 400 end users after reporting a greater than 10 percent reduction in after-hours documentation during the pilot.
items.contextSentence: Temple’s June 8, 2026 newsroom note names Slovis as CMIO for Temple University Hospital; the April PBJ sponsored article reported the after-hours documentation reduction that preceded the 400-user expansion.

items.title: CHOP publishes ORCA repo
items.dek: CHOP’s ORCA repository is an offline, read-only viewer for Epic order sets and SmartSets during downtime.
items.body:
Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia published ORCA, the Offsite Repository of Clinical Assets, as a public GitHub repository. The tool gives clinical teams an offline, read-only way to search Epic order sets and SmartSets during downtime.

ORCA is designed as a reference when the live EHR is unavailable. It contains no patient data and cannot place orders, preserving a clear safety boundary while giving clinicians access to standardized content during an outage.

CHOP credits Bimal Desai with conceiving the project and Stephon Proctor with building it. Desai and Hojjat Salmasian shared the repository on Aug. 3, and the repository points readers to related work published in Applied Clinical Informatics in 2025.
items.impactSentence: ORCA is an offline read-only Epic order-set viewer for downtime; it does not hold patient data and cannot place orders.
items.contextSentence: The public repository turns CHOP’s earlier Applied Clinical Informatics work on a read-only downtime viewer into an implementation other nonprofit health systems can examine.

items.title: Tower Health CIO on AI label, AI tax, and owned platforms
items.dek: Tower Health CIO Tom Bartiromo is requiring proof of measurable value before paying premiums for AI-labeled products.
items.body: Becker’s Hospital Review, July 23, 2026, quoted Tom Bartiromo, senior vice president and CIO of Tower Health in West Reading, Pa., on vendors putting an AI label on existing automation and charging an “AI tax.” He said the test is whether the product delivers a genuinely different outcome or is existing automation with an AI premium. He requires a proof-of-value engagement under real operating conditions, not vendor benchmarks. “A demonstration is not evidence,” he said. If the AI version does not produce a material, measurable improvement, he would keep the proven non-AI product at the original price. A second Becker’s clip, about July 30, 2026, quoted Bartiromo saying Tower is scrutinizing “AI-adjacent add-ons” more aggressively and that the emphasis is less about point solutions and more toward realizing more value from the core platforms it already owns. Vendors are to show measurable, system-level outcomes rather than feature-level promise.
items.impactSentence: Tower will not pay an AI premium without a proof-of-value under its own conditions, and it is pressing vendors for value from platforms it already owns.
items.contextSentence: The July 23 Becker’s AI-tax comments and the July 30 core-platform comments are separate clips from the same CIO.

items.title: Temple Health–Chestnut Hill Hospital and Jefferson Health Plans: contract scheduled to end Sept. 30, 2026
items.dek: Temple Health's Aug. 17, 2026 notice says the Medicaid and Medicare agreement ends Sept. 30. Starting Oct. 1, Jefferson Health Plans would not pay for care at that hospital if no new deal is reached. Emergency care stays covered. Pregnancy care continues. Ongoing or prior-authorized care can continue for up to 60 days after Sept. 30.
items.body:
On Aug. 17, 2026, Temple Health posted that Temple Health–Chestnut Hill Hospital's agreement with Jefferson Health Plans, a Medicaid and Medicare managed-care company, is scheduled to end Sept. 30, 2026. Temple wrote that the two sides have not yet reached a new agreement.

If there is no deal, Jefferson Health Plans would not pay for care at that hospital starting Oct. 1, 2026. The same notice lists exceptions: emergency care remains covered; pregnancy care at the hospital continues before and after birth; and patients with ongoing care for a condition treated there in the last 12 months, or with prior authorization, can keep getting that care for up to 60 days after Sept. 30, 2026.

Temple said Pennsylvania Medicaid members can change plans at any time through the PA Enrollment Center, with a new plan effective in 30 to 45 days. It said Medicare members qualify for a CMS Special Enrollment Period and can request a plan change as early as Sept. 1, 2026. Medicare Open Enrollment, the notice says, runs through Dec. 7, 2026.
items.impactSentence: Temple Health–Chestnut Hill Hospital's contract with Jefferson Health Plans is scheduled to end Sept. 30, 2026, and starting Oct. 1 Jefferson Health Plans would not pay for care there if no new agreement is reached.
items.contextSentence: The Sept. 30, 2026 end date is Temple Health’s Aug. 17, 2026 notice for Temple Health–Chestnut Hill Hospital only.

items.title: HAP June 10, 2025 letter: enforce CMS-0057-F; 1.6 million Pennsylvanians in Medicare Advantage
items.dek: HAP, for 235 institutions, asked CMS to enforce the Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule. The letter cites 54 percent of Pennsylvania Medicare beneficiaries, or 1.6 million people, in MA, and a 60 percent rise over ten years.
items.body:
On June 10, 2025, HAP told CMS Administrator Mehmet Oz it joins the AHA in asking CMS to enforce CMS-0057-F. Kate McCale, HAP vice president of compliance and regulatory affairs, signed for 235 institutions.

HAP wrote that 54 percent of Medicare beneficiaries in Pennsylvania, or 1.6 million people, are in Medicare Advantage, and that MA enrollment in the state rose 60 percent over the last ten years. It said members face delays and extra documentation with MA organizations on authorization and payment.

CMS's Jan. 17, 2024 fact sheet gives impacted payers until Jan. 1, 2027 for the FHIR APIs, including the Prior Authorization API. Decision clocks generally begin Jan. 1, 2026: 72 hours for expedited requests and seven calendar days for standard requests. The API requirements exclude drugs, and the decision-timeframe provision excludes FFE QHP issuers.

The same HAP letter says the TEAM model would apply to 26 Pennsylvania hospitals.
items.impactSentence: On June 10, 2025, HAP asked CMS to enforce the Interoperability and Prior Authorization Final Rule (CMS-0057-F), citing 1.6 million Pennsylvanians in Medicare Advantage (54 percent of the state's Medicare beneficiaries).
items.contextSentence: CMS’s Jan. 17, 2024 fact sheet gives impacted payers until Jan. 1, 2027 for the FHIR APIs; HAP’s June 10, 2025 letter asks CMS to enforce that rule.

items.title: QGenda QuickLinks showed on-call schedules and clinician cell numbers at Penn, CHOP, and ChristianaCare
items.dek: The Inquirer, Aug. 31, 2026, reported public QGenda landing pages for those three systems and nearly 50 hospitals nationally. No patient PHI. Philly systems pulled the links in late August after the paper alerted them.
items.body:
The Philadelphia Inquirer, Aug. 31, 2026, 1:27 p.m. ET (Abraham Gutman, Sarah Gantz), reported that QGenda QuickLinks publicly displayed months of on-call schedules and cell phone numbers for thousands of workers at Penn Medicine, Children’s Hospital of Philadelphia, ChristianaCare, and nearly 50 health systems or hospitals nationwide, including Veterans Affairs hospitals. The paper said the pages were not in Google search results but could be retrieved with AI tools, including OpenAI’s Codex. It said QGenda, an Atlanta-based Hearst-owned workforce vendor, did not respond to comment requests.

QGenda’s own site advertises QuickLinks so “any staff member without a QGenda account” can bookmark a live provider schedule, and separately says landing pages can be IP-restricted so only devices on a practice’s secure network can see public-facing schedule data.

The Inquirer said Philly-area systems took the pages down in late August after it alerted them. A ChristianaCare spokesperson said the system recently became aware the pages were public, immediately worked with QGenda to eliminate the vulnerability, and was not aware of any impact to caregivers, clinicians, patient care, or operations. CHOP told staff last week it was updating access to QGenda on-call displays “out of an abundance of caution”; a CHOP spokesperson said the platform does not contain patient information. Penn said it uses QGenda for care-team communication and is adding controls. Penn and CHOP did not answer whether they knew the links were reachable without a login. Other Philadelphia-area systems did not appear to have public links.
items.impactSentence: Penn, CHOP, and ChristianaCare pulled public QGenda QuickLinks in late August after the Inquirer showed they displayed on-call schedules and clinician cell numbers without a login; CHOP said the platform holds no patient information.
items.contextSentence: QGenda documents QuickLinks for unauthenticated staff and an optional IP restriction on public landing pages.

items.dek: HealthShare Exchange recertified HITRUST r2 for its hosting systems and data integration tools, with evidence against 536 controls. HSX has held HITRUST certification since 2017.
items.body: On June 2, 2026, HealthShare Exchange said its hosting systems and data integration tools renewed HITRUST r2 certification. The recertification cited evidence against 536 controls. HSX has maintained HITRUST-certified status since 2017. Alice Vuong, vice president and chief information security officer, said the certification is a continuous organizational effort to safeguard health data moving across Pennsylvania, New Jersey, and Delaware.
items.impactSentence: HSX recertified HITRUST r2 on June 2, 2026 for hosting and data-integration systems, citing 536 controls and certification held since 2017.

items.title: Anna Schoenbaum: Penn ambient documentation scale
items.dek: Penn Medicine’s chief digital applications officer said ambient documentation covers about 1,300 ambulatory providers and over 600 nurses, with a 20% documentation-time reduction and decreased after-hours documentation for 79% of users.
items.body: In an Aug. 18, 2026 HealthTech Magazine interview, Anna Schoenbaum, vice president and chief digital applications officer at Penn Medicine, said Penn’s ambient documentation covers approximately 1,300 ambulatory providers and over 600 nurses. She reported a 20% reduction in documentation time and decreased after-hours documentation for 79% of users, with full-scale deployment targeted for fall 2026.
items.role: VP and Chief Digital Applications Officer
items.impactSentence: Schoenbaum said Penn ambient documentation covers about 1,300 ambulatory providers and 600+ nurses, with 20% less note time and less after-hours documentation for 79% of users.

items.title: Anahi Santiago: home-based care expands cloud security
items.dek: ChristianaCare’s CISO said hospital-at-home and home-based care move more patient data into cloud environments, expanding what security teams have to protect.
items.body: In a June 29, 2026 Information Security Media Group interview, Anahi Santiago, CISO at ChristianaCare, said hospital-at-home and home-based care require patient data to leave hospital walls and move into cloud environments. She said that shift expands the volume of sensitive information her team must protect across public, private, and software-as-a-service platforms.
items.impactSentence: ChristianaCare’s CISO said home-based care moves more patient data into the cloud, expanding the security surface her team has to protect.

items.title: ACHE of Greater Philadelphia 2026 Fall Symposium
items.body: ACHE of Greater Philadelphia’s 2026 Fall Symposium is Monday, Sept. 14 at the Smilow Center for Translational Research, 3400 Civic Center Boulevard, Philadelphia. Breakfast and registration open at 7:00 a.m.; the program runs 8:00 a.m. to 4:30 p.m. Registration closes Sept. 6. Programming is sponsored by the Clinical Practices of the University of Pennsylvania and Aya Healthcare. Official panels cover physician leadership, data and advanced analytics, the inpatient-to-ambulatory shift, and legislative issues facing healthcare leaders.

items.title: HAP Emergency Management Conference: Security. Continuity. Resilience.
items.body: HAP’s Sept. 16, 2026 Emergency Management Conference is at the Holiday Inn Harrisburg Hershey in Grantville. Registration opens at 8:00 a.m., the program begins at 9:00 a.m., and the agenda adjourns at 3:45 p.m. Although the venue is outside the Valley, official sessions directly feature Penn Medicine Chester County Hospital and Penn Medicine associate CHIO Joy Iocca on standardized EHR-downtime continuity; Tower Health system director of security Brian Swearingen on AI and analytics for hospital security; and Lower Bucks Hospital leaders on the Bristol Township nursing-home explosion response.
